extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in psychology and cognitive neuroscience of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Suls' two-stage model for appreciation of jokes and cartoons (detection and resolution of incongruity), discusses neural correlates, modality effects (verbal vs nonverbal), and cognitive-resource influences on perceived funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity is generated when a prediction is not confirmed in the final part of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first stage in Suls' two-stage model: the joke or cartoon must create a mismatch between an expectation and the actual outcome (prediction violation) for humor comprehension to begin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of incongruity (reinterpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To comprehend humor, it is necessary to revisit the story, transforming an incongruous situation into a funny, congruous one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second stage requires reanalysis or mental restructuring so that the prior incongruity is explained; successful resolution is what permits the incongruity to be experienced as humorous rather than merely confusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction-violation as source of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises when an initial prediction about a narrative or situation is not confirmed by its final part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective jokes/cartoons set up expectations that are then violated in a way that allows for reinterpretation; assessing whether a work creates a clear prediction that can be overturned is central to evaluating its humorous potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution-of-intention as a mechanism for resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolution of incongruity might occur through a process of intention attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author hypothesizes that understanding others' intentions (theory-of-mind processes) can provide the reinterpretation needed to resolve incongruity; nonverbal tasks that probe attribution of intention show overlapping neural activation with humor resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional response / subjective amusement (amygdala involvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective ratings of funniness correlate with activation of the left amygdala, suggesting the amygdala gives humor an emotional dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure funniness via subjective ratings and consider emotional engagement as a distinct criterion: cognitive resolution is necessary but the emotional reaction (amusement) is reflected in limbic activation and contributes to the overall appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality effects: verbal vs nonverbal stimuli
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent activation of the left hemisphere due to language processing, the authors used a nonverbal task comprising cartoon pairs; both left and right hemispheres were activated when comparing funny versus nonfunny cartoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing studies of humor, consider stimulus modality: nonverbal cartoons can isolate nonlinguistic humor-processing and reveal bilateral neural contributions; modality influences how language processing might confound hemispheric findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hemispheric involvement and neural loci
rubrics_metrics.description: Patient studies found right brain-lesion patients have difficulties in humor comprehension, whereas neuroimaging studies suggest major involvement of the left hemisphere; for funny vs nonfunny cartoons both hemispheres showed activation (right inferior frontal gyrus BA47; left superior temporal gyrus BA38; left middle temporal gyrus BA21; left cerebellum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use converging evidence (patient data and imaging) when attributing neural mechanisms; specific regional activations can be treated as indicators of detection, resolution, and affective processing stages in humor appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive-resource / task-load effects on humor perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects who engaged in a taxing cognitive task perceived complex captioned cartoons to be less humorous than those who engaged in an easy task; task complexity had little effect on perceived humor of simple or political captioned cartoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how cognitive load and stimulus complexity interact: complex jokes requiring more processing are more sensitive to reduced cognitive resources; consider cognitive demands of a joke/cartoon when predicting or measuring its perceived funniness.
